propositions.text: The appellants are Nigerian and US citizens appealing the RPD's refugee protection denial.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant), her spouse, XXXX XXXX (the male Appellant), and their children, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX (the minor Appellants, respectively), all citizens of Republic of Nigeria, and XXXX XXXX XXXX, (a minor Appellant) a citizen of the United States of America, are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection.

propositions.text: The male appellant remains the designated representative for minor children under RAD Rule 23(1).
propositions.quote: The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) assumes that the (male) Appellant has remained the designated representative (DR) for their minor children as the designation of the DR at the RPD is deemed to continue for a RAD appeal under RAD Rule 23(1).

propositions.text: No new evidence was submitted in support of the appeal.
propositions.quote: They have submitted no new evidence in support of their appeal.

propositions.text: The appellants ask the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and substitute a positive decision or refer for redetermination by a different panel.
propositions.quote: The Appellants ask the RAD to set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute its own positive decision, or to refer her claim to the RPD for redetermination by a differently-constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellants, Nigerian and US citizens, appeal the RPD denial, with no new evidence, seeking a positive decision or referral; the male appellant remains representative.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA s.111(1)(a), the RAD confirms the RPD's decision that appellants are not refugees or in need of protection and dismisses the appeal.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellants are not Convention refugees nor are they persons in need of protection. The RAD dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD's decision under IRPA and dismisses the appeal.

propositions.text: Appellants alleged male appellant's family consider principal appellant and daughter witches and subject females to rituals including FGM.
propositions.quote: The Appellants alleged before the RPD that family members of the male Appellant consider the principal Appellant and her daughter to be witches. The Appellants further allege before the RPD that as a result of this accusation they are being requested to undergo rituals, which include the females being subjected to Female Genital Mutilation (FGM).

propositions.text: Appellants allege a well-founded fear of persecution due to these accusations and rituals.
propositions.quote: The Appellants further allege as a result they have a well-founded fear of persecution.

propositions.text: Their Basis of Claim form, narrative and documents express their fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: The Appellants indicate that their Basis of Claim (BoC) form, narrative and supporting documents speak of their fear of persecution.

propositions.text: Appellants left Nigeria in 2015 and made an inland refugee claim in Canada the same year.
propositions.quote: The Appellants left Nigeria on XXXX XXXX, 2015 and made an inland claim for refugee protection on XXXX XXXX, 2015 in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants alleged witchcraft accusations and FGM rituals causing fear of persecution, supported by their claim forms; they left Nigeria and claimed in Canada in 2015.

propositions.text: RPD hearings occurred in December 2015 and January 2016; decision rejecting claims issued January 26, 2016.
propositions.quote: The Appellants had their refugee determination hearings on December 21, 2015 and January 14, 2016. In a written decision issued on January 26, 2016 the RPD rejected the claims.

propositions.text: RPD found male appellant excluded under Article 1F(b) and others had a viable internal flight alternative in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: The RPD member found that the male Appellant was excluded pursuant to Article 1F (b) and the other Appellants had a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD held hearings in late 2015 and rejected claims, excluding the male appellant and finding others had an internal flight alternative.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred in IFA analysis, ignored relevant evidence, and appeal can succeed on new evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its IFA analysis, that the RPD ignored or failed to take relevant evidence into consideration, and that the appeal can succeed on the basis of new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the RPD erred on internal flight alternative and evidence, and that new evidence supports appeal success.

propositions.text: Minister intervened at RPD hearing to find male appellant excluded under Article 1F(b).
propositions.quote: The Minister's representative, the "Minister", intervened in the RPD hearing asking the RPD to find that the male Appellant is an excluded person, pursuant to article 1F (b).

propositions.text: Minister did not intervene at the RAD appeal.
propositions.quote: The Minister did not intervene at the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister intervened at RPD to exclude the male appellant but did not intervene at the RAD appeal.

propositions.text: IRPA sets appeal grounds and remedies but does not specify RAD's standard of review for RPD decisions.
propositions.quote: While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes IRPA sets appeal grounds but not the RAD's standard of review for RPD decisions.

propositions.text: Appellants' counsel made no submissions on the appropriate standard of review for the RAD.
propositions.quote: The Appellants' counsel makes no submissions on the appropriate standard of review which is to be used by the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants' counsel did not submit on the appropriate standard of review for the RAD.

propositions.text: It is settled law that the RAD is not to review RPD decisions like a judicial review.
propositions.quote: It is settled law that the RAD is not to review decisions of the RPD in the manner of a judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court states settled law that the RAD does not review RPD decisions as a judicial review.

propositions.text: The RAD appeal is based on the RPD decision record unless new evidence is accepted and focuses on alleged errors of law, fact, or mixed fact and law.
propositions.quote: Such an appeal: "(i) is directed at the decision of the RPD; (ii) unless new evidence is accepted, is to be entertained on the basis of the record as it was constituted at the time of the RPD's decision; and (iii) is to be concerned solely with the errors of law, of fact or of mixed fact and law that, according to the appellant, the RPD made. This is the statutory configuration of an appeal before the RAD."

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the RAD appeal focuses on RPD decision record and alleged errors of law, fact, or mixed fact and law.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal states RAD must analyze RPD decision and provide final determination or refer back if oral evidence needed.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal in its decision clearly states, that the RAD is to carefully consider the RPD's decision and then carry out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred in its decision. The RAD is then to provide a final determination, either confirming the RPD's decision or setting it aside and substituting the RAD's own determination of the refugee claim. If the RAD cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence already presented to the RPD, the matter can be referred back to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal says the RAD must analyze the RPD decision and provide a final determination or refer back if needed.

propositions.text: RAD applies correctness standard to RPD findings of fact and mixed fact and law, undertaking its own analysis and substituting its view if it disagrees.
propositions.quote: When the RAD is dealing with the findings of fact and of mixed fact and law, the RAD is to review the RPD's decision applying a standard of correctness. When applying that standard, the RAD will not show deference to the RPD's reasoning process; it will rather undertake its own analysis of the question. The analysis will bring the RAD to choose whether it agrees with the determination of the RPD; if not, then RAD will substitute its own view and provide the correct answer.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applies correctness standard to RPD findings of fact and mixed fact and law, substituting its own view if it disagrees.

propositions.text: RPD has advantage in credibility findings from oral evidence; Federal Court of Appeal declined to define RAD's deference scope.
propositions.quote: However, there are cases where the RPD enjoys an expressive advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, as such findings require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to oral evidence heard by the RPD. The Federal Court of Appeal, in deliberating the standard of review to be applied by the RAD to the RPD's decision, has declined to provide the scope and degree of deference to be shown by the RAD: "The RAD should be given the opportunity to develop its own jurisprudence in that respect; there is no need for me to pigeon-hole the RAD to the level of deference owed in each case."

paragraphs.summary: The RPD has advantage in credibility findings from oral evidence; the Federal Court declined to define RAD's deference scope.

propositions.text: Federal Court notes consensus that RAD owes deference to RPD credibility findings without hearing, but level and scope of deference vary.
propositions.quote: As the Federal Court observed in Akuffo: "[T]here also appears to be a consensus that when no hearing is held before the RAD, the latter owes deference to the RPD's credibility findings. The opinions rather diverge on: i) the level of deference that is owed or its exact definition; and ii) the scope of the questions of fact and questions of mixed fact and law for which deference is owed."

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court notes consensus that RAD owes deference to RPD credibility findings without hearing, but level and scope vary.

propositions.text: RAD defers to RPD findings where RPD had advantage from oral testimony or specialized knowledge, including credibility and personal documents questioned.
propositions.quote: The RAD will show deference to the RPD's findings where the RPD was in an advantageous position to reach such conclusions. The RPD's advantage comes from seeing claimants and witnesses and hearing oral testimony from those individuals. Therefore, credibility findings which arise from that oral testimony are appropriate of deference, as are other findings of fact based on oral evidence, so are findings based on the RPD's specialized knowledge of a particular matter where the RAD does not have its own specialized knowledge with respect to the same factual issue. The RPD's advantage may even extend to personal documents in situations where it has questioned the claimant or witness about such documents and where the resulting testimony gives rise to credibility concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD defers to RPD findings where RPD had advantage from oral testimony or specialized knowledge, including credibility and personal documents.

propositions.text: Not all credibility findings warrant deference; implausibility or inferences based on reasoning or documents may not merit deference.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that not every finding relating to credibility however, warrants deference. Where the RPD has made a finding of implausibility, for example, it has no advantage where the determination of plausibility is based on the RPD's own reasoning, or on objective documents, and does not arise directly from the oral evidence. Similarly, where the RPD draws an inference - a credibility finding based on deduction and reasoning, rather than a contradiction in evidence - here the RAD may see no reason to show deference, as the appellate tribunal can be expected to have equal expertise in the inferential process.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD states not all credibility findings warrant deference, especially implausibility or inferences from reasoning or documents.

propositions.text: In Huruglica, Federal Court held RAD can respect RPD credibility conclusions but is not restricted to intervene only on palpable and overriding error.
propositions.quote: In Huruglica, the Federal Court held that the RAD can "recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is a 'palpable and overriding error'."

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court in Huruglica held RAD can respect RPD credibility conclusions but is not limited to intervening only on palpable and overriding error.

propositions.text: The RAD believes 'recognize and respect' means a reasonableness standard, as Federal Court upheld RAD decisions applying reasonableness.
propositions.quote: It is unfortunate that the Federal Court did not explain what level of deference is established by recognizing and respecting a conclusion of the RPD, it has repeatedly upheld decisions in which the RAD applied a reasonableness standard to decisions of the RPD. This leads the RAD to believe, this proposes that "recognize and respect" is indeed somewhat similar to reasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD believes 'recognize and respect' means a reasonableness standard, based on Federal Court decisions.

propositions.text: Dunsmuir discusses deferential review elements: process and outcome; RAD finds this framework helpful despite differences.
propositions.quote: In Dunsmuir, the Supreme Court discussed two elements of a deferential review: process and outcome. Despite the difference between judicial review and a RAD appeal, the RAD finds this framework helpful in considering its own approach to deference.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Dunsmuir framework of process and outcome helpful for its approach to deference.

propositions.text: Deferential RAD review requires RPD findings to result from intelligible reasoning that the RAD can comprehend.
propositions.quote: Where the RAD is to show deference to findings of the RPD, those findings must still be the result of an intelligible reasoning process. The RAD must be able to read the RPD's decision and comprehend how the RPD's conclusions were reached.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD states that deferential review requires RPD findings to have intelligible reasoning the RAD can understand.

propositions.text: The RAD's outcome must be based on and supported by the evidence before the RPD.
propositions.quote: the outcome of that process must be a product that is based on and supported by the evidence that was before the RPD

propositions.text: The RAD must review the RPD's evidence to conclude if the RPD's outcome is supported by that evidence.
propositions.quote: it is principally important that the RAD employ its own review of the evidence in the RPD's record, in order to conclude whether the RPD's outcome is supported by that evidence

paragraphs.summary: The RAD must base its outcome on evidence before the RPD and review that evidence to confirm the RPD's outcome is supported, says the court.

propositions.text: The RAD applies a standard of correctness and conducts its own review and analysis of the RPD's decision.
propositions.quote: The RAD will apply a standard of correctness to its consideration of the RPD's decision: it will conduct its own review of the evidence and undertake its own analysis of the question

propositions.text: If the RAD's review does not lead to the same conclusion as the RPD, the RPD's finding is wrong.
propositions.quote: If this does not lead the RAD to the same conclusion as the RPD, the RPD's finding is wrong

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applies correctness standard and if it disagrees with the RPD, the RPD's finding is wrong, says the court.

propositions.text: The RAD will not interfere with RPD findings based on RPD's distinct advantages or intelligible reasoning embedded in those advantages.
propositions.quote: the RAD will not interfere with the RPD's findings where such conclusions result from the RPD's distinct advantages or from a intelligible reasoning process whose premises are embedded in such advantages

propositions.text: If the RPD's process or conclusion does not meet these requirements, the RAD will find the findings in error.
propositions.quote: If either the process or the conclusion does not meet these requirements, the RAD will determine the findings to be in error

paragraphs.summary: The RAD defers to RPD's findings based on distinct advantages and intelligible reasoning, else finds error, says the court.

propositions.text: The RAD will confirm or set aside the RPD's decision or refer back for redetermination if oral evidence is needed.
propositions.quote: the RAD will provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD's decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination. If it cannot do so without hearing oral evidence that was already heard by the RPD, it will refer the matter back for redetermination

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will confirm, set aside, or refer back the RPD decision if oral evidence is needed, says the court.

propositions.text: The Panel erred in its analysis of the exclusion clause under Article 1F (b).
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the Panel erred in its analysis of the exclusion clause under Article 1F (b)

propositions.text: The Panel found the male Appellant excluded for serious non-political crime.
propositions.quote: The Panel determined that the male Appellant was excluded from protection as there were serious reasons for considering that the Appellant committed a serious non-political crime

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue the Panel erred on Article 1F(b) exclusion; the Panel found the male Appellant excluded for serious non-political crime.

propositions.text: The Minister bears the burden to prove exclusion under section 98 IRPA and Article 1F(b).
propositions.quote: The burden is on the Minister to make a case for exclusion before the RPD that the Appellant is excluded from refugee protection pursuant to section 98 of the IRPA and Section F(b) of Article 1 of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees

paragraphs.summary: The Minister must prove exclusion under section 98 IRPA and Article 1F(b), says the court.

propositions.text: The Appellant's arrest in the USA for fraud and forged documents supports serious non-political crime exclusion.
propositions.quote: The Minister also submitted that the Appellant's testimony and documentary evidence regarding his arrest in the United States of America for Fraud and Use, trafficking or possession of forged document supports a finding of serious reasons for considering that the claimant has committed a serious, non-political crime

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues the Appellant's US arrest for fraud and forged documents supports exclusion for serious non-political crime.

propositions.text: Exclusion is not supportable; the Appellant's actions were not serious under Article 1F(b).
propositions.quote: The Appellant's counsel in submissions stated that a finding of exclusion on such basis is not supportable, his actions were not serious within the context of Article 1F (b)

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant's counsel argues exclusion is not supportable as actions were not serious under Article 1F(b).

propositions.text: Conviction for fraud and forged document offences are serious crimes given maximum penalties of 10-14 years.
propositions.quote: I disagree with the Appellants' submission that "conviction for Fraud and Use, trafficking or possession of forged document," is not a serious offence. The fact that the penalty for Fraud carries a maximum of 14 years and the other two carry maximum penalties of 10 years, this strongly suggests that Canada does consider such crimes to be "serious"

propositions.text: Canada considers crimes punishable by at least 10 years as serious, per Federal Court of Appeal in Jayasekara.
propositions.quote: As stated by the Federal Court of Appeal in Jayasekara, "while regard should be had to international standards, the perspective of the receiving state or nation cannot be ignored in determining the seriousness of the crime"

propositions.text: The crimes in question are serious as punishable by maximum sentences of 10-14 years in Canada.
propositions.quote: the fact that the crimes of Fraud and Use, trafficking or possession of forged document is punishable by a maximum sentence of fourteen years for Fraud and ten years for the other two strongly suggests that they are crimes that Canada considers to be "serious"

paragraphs.summary: The court finds fraud and forged document offences serious given 10-14 year penalties, citing Jayasekara on Canada's perspective.

propositions.text: Evidence supports exclusion for serious criminality under Article 1F(b) for acts before entering Canada.
propositions.quote: The Minister argues that on the facts presently before the RAD as they were before the RPD, there is sufficient evidence to support a finding of exclusion by the Panel for serious criminality under Article 1F (b)

propositions.text: The male Appellant was convicted in Massachusetts for credit card fraud and sentenced to prison, probation, and restitution.
propositions.quote: the male Appellant was convicted in the USA in the State of Massachusetts on "credit card fraud" and sentenced to 20 months in prison, three years' probation and pay restitution in the amount of $14,020

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues evidence supports exclusion for serious crime; the court finds male Appellant convicted in Massachusetts for credit card fraud.

propositions.text: The RPD gave clear and full reasons for its finding of exclusion.
propositions.quote: The RPD provided very clear and fulsome reasons on how it arrived at its finding

propositions.text: The RAD concurs with the RPD's findings on exclusion.
propositions.quote: The RAD has assessed the RPD findings and concurs with the RPD findings

paragraphs.summary: The RPD gave clear reasons for exclusion; the RAD concurs with the RPD's findings, says the court.

propositions.text: The RPD had serious credibility concerns about adult Appellants' police report dealings.
propositions.quote: the RPD had serious concerns about the credibility of the adult Appellants regarding their dealings with filing police reports

propositions.text: The claimant omitted that a police commissioner friend said FGM is a family matter and police would not investigate.
propositions.quote: The panel also finds that the claimant omitted from his narrative that he later called a friend who is a police commissioner XXXX who confirmed to the male claimant that he issued of FGM is a family matter and the police would not investigate matter

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found credibility concerns about Appellants' police report dealings and omissions about police commissioner's statement, says the court.

propositions.text: The RAD concurs with the RPD that credible evidence supports excluding the male Appellant for serious non-political criminality before Canada entry.
propositions.quote: the RAD concurs with the RPD's finding that there is sufficient credible evidence on which to find that the male Appellant is an excluded person due to alleged serious non-political criminality prior to his entry into Canada

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concurs with the RPD that credible evidence excludes the male Appellant for serious non-political crime before entry, says the court.

propositions.text: The male Appellant is excluded under Article 1F(b) and section 98 IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the male Appellant is an excluded person, as per Article 1F (b) and section 98 of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the male Appellant excluded under Article 1F(b) and section 98 IRPA, says the court.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellants have a reasonable IFA in Abuja, Benin State or Port Harcourt.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellants have a reasonable IFA in Abuja, Benin State or Port Harcourt

propositions.text: The Appellants argue the RPD should have analyzed their subjective fear more thoroughly.
propositions.quote: The Appellants plead that the RPD should have carried out a thorough analysis of their subjective fear

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found a reasonable IFA; the Appellants argue the RPD should have analyzed their subjective fear more thoroughly.

propositions.text: The RPD must apply a two-pronged test to assess IFA viability, which it did.
propositions.quote: When assessing the viability of an IFA, the RPD must apply a two-pronged test. The RPD followed this approach

propositions.text: The two-pronged test for IFA is based on Rasaratnam and Thirunavukkarasu cases.
propositions.quote: The basis for this two-pronged test is the cases of Rasaratnam and Thirunavukkarasu

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD applied the two-pronged IFA test based on Rasaratnam and Thirunavukkarasu cases.

propositions.text: The Board must be satisfied on balance of probabilities that no serious persecution risk exists in the IFA.
propositions.quote: The Board must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists

paragraphs.summary: The Board must be satisfied on balance of probabilities that no serious persecution risk exists in the IFA, says the court.

propositions.text: Conditions in the IFA must make it reasonable for the claimant to seek refuge there, considering all circumstances.
propositions.quote: Conditions in that part of the country considered being an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him or her to seek refuge there

paragraphs.summary: Conditions in the IFA must make it reasonable for the claimant to seek refuge there, says the court.

propositions.text: The RAD will apply the two-pronged approach to the IFA.
propositions.quote: The RAD will apply this two-pronged approach

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will apply the two-pronged approach to the IFA, says the court.

propositions.text: The RPD found no supporting documentation that the Appellants' elderly uncle is a well-known influential public figure in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant did not disclose any supporting documentation to establish that the Appellants' elderly uncle, the agents of persecution, is well-known public figures in Nigeria who wield any degree of influence of power in Nigeria

propositions.text: The RPD found no evidence that the elderly uncle is a popular herbalist consulting politicians, police, and military officers.
propositions.quote: In particular, the RPD found that the Appellant provided no documentation to support the allegation that his elderly uncle is a popular and public figure in Nigeria who consults as an herbalist with politicians, police officers and military officers

propositions.text: The RPD found no documentary evidence that the elderly uncle has wealth or police connections.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellants provided no documentary evidence to establish that his elderly uncle who has the wealth or connections to the police

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no evidence that the Appellants' elderly uncle is a well-known influential figure or herbalist with police connections, says the court.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal in Maldonado creates presumption that sworn facts are true unless valid reason to doubt
propositions.quote: the Federal Court of Appeal, in Maldonado,26 states that when a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true unless there is valid reason to doubt their truthfulness.

propositions.text: RPD did not provide valid reasons to doubt truthfulness of influence of agents of persecution
propositions.quote: The Appellants plead that the RPD did not provide valid reasons to doubt the truthfulness of the influence of the agents of persecution.

propositions.text: Federal Court warns against rejecting claim solely for lack of corroborative evidence
propositions.quote: The Appellants also referred to the jurisprudence where the Federal Court has warned against rejecting a claim based solely on the lack of corroborative evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue the RPD lacked valid reasons to doubt their sworn facts and warn against rejecting claims solely for lack of corroboration, citing Federal Court jurisprudence.

propositions.text: RPD had no reason to doubt Appellant's evidence about photographs given to Nigerian police
propositions.quote: The Appellants plead that the RPD had no reason to doubt the Appellant's evidence on the point surrounding their photographs being furnished to police in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue the RPD had no reason to doubt their evidence about photographs given to Nigerian police.

propositions.text: RAD agrees with the RPD for stated reasons
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees with the RPD for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with the RPD's decision for reasons to follow.

propositions.text: Corroborative evidence can reasonably be expected in this case
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, for the following reasons, that in the case at hand, corroborative evidence can be reasonably expected.

propositions.text: BOC form instructs Appellants to provide supporting documents
propositions.quote: The Basis of Claim (BOC) form clearly instructs the Appellants to provide "any documents you have to support your claim".

propositions.text: Appellant had contact with family in Nigeria after arriving in Canada and time to obtain documentary evidence
propositions.quote: According to the Appellant's BOC narrative and his oral testimony before the RPD, the Appellant had contact with family members in Nigeria after he arrived in Canada.

propositions.text: No evidence Appellant tried to obtain supporting evidence about agents of persecution
propositions.quote: yet there was no evidence adduced that they made any attempts to obtain any supporting evidence.

propositions.text: Nigeria is large with over 900,000 sq km and 180 million population
propositions.quote: Given the size of Nigeria both in area and population, an area of over 900,000 square kilometers and a population of over 180 million,

propositions.text: Critical to establish profile of agents of persecution who could find Appellants in Nigeria
propositions.quote: the RAD finds it critical to establish the profile of agents of persecution who could find the Appellants in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds corroborative evidence reasonably expected; Appellant had time and contact to obtain it but did not, and Nigeria's size makes profiling agents critical.

propositions.text: Appellant testified elderly uncle and family rely on him financially
propositions.quote: According to the recording of the hearing, the Appellant testified that his elderly uncle as other members of his family relied upon him giving them money.

propositions.text: Family lacks resources or authority to search for Appellants
propositions.quote: This evidence clearly indicates that the male Appellant's family lacks the resources to be able to have any authority with the police or anyone else to conduct a search for the whereabouts of the Appellants.

propositions.text: No evidence about uncle's profile or efforts to obtain evidence regarding him
propositions.quote: The male Appellant did not provide any evidence of his uncle's profile such as his work and status in the country. No evidence was adduced if he had made any efforts to obtain evidence regarding his elderly uncle

propositions.text: Appellant's responses about efforts to obtain evidence were vague and unfruitful
propositions.quote: The RAD finds these responses or lack of were vague and provide no information regarding efforts made to obtain evidence and why the efforts were not fruitful.

propositions.text: RPD asked how uncle/family might find Appellants in large city; Appellant did not answer directly
propositions.quote: The RPD asked the Appellant how his uncle and family might find the Appellants if they were in Port Harcourt, a city with millions of people. The Appellant testified that he sometimes appeared on television, but did not directly answer the question.

propositions.text: RAD may reject speculative inferences even without adverse credibility finding
propositions.quote: The RAD is entitled to reject some or all of the inferences drawn by an Appellant, especially if they are speculative in nature, even in the absence of an adverse finding of credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant's family lacks resources to search, no evidence of efforts to obtain evidence, vague responses, and speculative inferences may be rejected.

propositions.text: Appellant testified he is known in Nigeria from TV but gave no support
propositions.quote: According to the recording of the hearing the Appellant testified that he is known throughout Nigeria as he sometimes appears on television, but provided nothing to support this.

propositions.text: Appellant's uncle and family live in Ibadan but no explanation how they could trace Appellants
propositions.quote: The Appellant explained that his uncle and family reside in Ibadan but not how he would be able to trace them anywhere in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Appellant's testimony on uncle's ability to trace them lacked sufficient detail
propositions.quote: the RAD founds the Appellant's testimony regarding his uncle ability to trace them to be lacking in sufficient detail.

propositions.text: RPD asked how uncle would find Appellants in Abuja or Port Harcourt; Appellant gave unsatisfactory answers
propositions.quote: The RPD asked the Appellant how the elderly uncle would find the Appellants if they resided in Abuja, or Port Harcourt. The Appellant testified that due to his business he would have to work and the children would have to attend school, further if it became known that his wife was a witch, they would be killed.

propositions.text: RAD finds explanation unsatisfactory and question inadequately answered
propositions.quote: The RAD finds this explanation unsatisfactory, as the questions was not adequately answered.

propositions.text: Unlikely people in Port Harcourt or Abuja would know or recognize Appellants as witch allegation is local
propositions.quote: The RAD finds it highly unlikely that people in Port Harcourt or Abuja would know or recognize the Appellants in the IFAs, as the allegation of the principal Appellant being a witch is a local issue.

propositions.text: People in Port Harcourt or Abuja would not know about witch allegation unless told by Appellants
propositions.quote: The people of Port Harcourt or Abuja would not know anything about the allegation against the principal Appellant unless they were told by the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant's testimony about being known and uncle's tracing ability unsupported, unsatisfactory, and unlikely to lead to recognition in large cities.

propositions.text: Appellants have not established on balance of probabilities they would be tracked or targeted in Abuja or Port Harcourt
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, on the basis of the evidence before it, that the Appellants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that they would be tracked down or targeted in Abuja, or Port Harcourt.

propositions.text: Lack of evidence on influence and reach of elderly uncle as agent of persecution
propositions.quote: Given the lack of evidence presented related to the influence and reach of the elderly uncles, the agent of persecution,

propositions.text: Appellants have not adduced sufficient evidence of serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment in Abuja or Port Harcourt
propositions.quote: the RAD finds that the Appellants have not adduced sufficient evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that there is a serious possibility of being persecuted in the IFA cities or that they would be personally subjected to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in Abuja, or Port Harcourt.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellants failed to prove on balance of probabilities a serious possibility of persecution or risk in Abuja or Port Harcourt.

propositions.text: RAD considered Nigerian Police Force's interest and ability to apprehend Appellants in IFAs
propositions.quote: The RAD has, therefore, considered the interest and the ability of the Nigerian Police Force (NPF) to apprehend the Appellants in the IFA locales.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD considered the Nigerian Police Force's ability and interest to apprehend the Appellants in the IFAs.

propositions.text: Appellants have been out of Nigeria over one year with no persuasive evidence of high profile or police search
propositions.quote: The Appellants have been out of Nigeria for over one year. They provided no persuasive evidence that they have high profiles and no persuasive evidence that the NPF are looking for them throughout the country.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence of large resourceful group searching for Appellants in Abuja or Port Harcourt
propositions.quote: There is no persuasive evidence that there is a large resourceful group of people in Nigeria, a country of over 180 million31 people, who are searching of would continue to search for the Appellants and seek them out in Abuja, or Port Harcourt.

propositions.text: Population of Abuja is more than 2.5 million
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the population of Abuja is more than 2.5 million.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no persuasive evidence Appellants are high profile or being searched for in Nigeria, noting Abuja's large population.

propositions.text: UK Home Office report states Nigerian constitution provides freedom of movement and residence
propositions.quote: A report from the United Kingdom Home Office states that the 1999 Nigerian constitution provides for the freedom of movement within Nigeria, and states that every citizen of Nigeria is entitled to move freely throughout Nigeria and to reside in any part thereof, and no citizen of Nigeria shall be expelled from Nigeria or refused entry thereto or exit therefrom.

propositions.text: International airports in Abuja and Port Harcourt; authorities need not be advised of return
propositions.quote: There are international airports in Abuja and Port Harcourt. The RAD notes the obvious fact that the Nigerian authorities do not have to be advised about the Appellants' return to the country and would, therefore, have no knowledge of their whereabouts in any of these cities.

propositions.text: No reason to believe Appellants' location would be found if they do not inform others
propositions.quote: if the Appellants do not wish to inform others of their presence in any of the IFAs, there is no reason to believe that their location would be found out.

propositions.text: Appellants failed to explain why they believe they would be discovered or harmed in IFAs
propositions.quote: Thus, the Appellants have failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why they believe they would be discovered and/or harmed in any of the three IFAs.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes Nigerian constitutional freedom of movement, airports, and finds no reason Appellants would be found or harmed if they keep location secret.

propositions.text: Appellants provided no persuasive evidence they are of nation-wide interest to Nigerian Police Force
propositions.quote: The Appellants provided no persuasive evidence that they are a matter of nation-wide interest to the NPF.

propositions.text: RAD not persuaded NPF are searching for Appellants throughout Nigeria
propositions.quote: The RAD is not persuaded that the NPF throughout the country are searching for the Appellants.

propositions.text: UK Home Office report: NPF is principal law enforcement with 350,000+ personnel covering all states and Abuja
propositions.quote: A report from the UK Home Office indicates that the NPF is the principal law enforcement agency in Nigeria with more than 350,000 men and women. NPF is a federal police force covering all 36 Nigerian states and the federal capital territory, Abuja.

propositions.text: NPF suffers serious lack of resources undermining effectiveness
propositions.quote: The report states that a serious lack of resources, including communications equipment, vehicles, skilled leadership, and training, continued to undermine the effectiveness of the NPF.

propositions.text: Reports of police asking victims for vehicles or money for fuel
propositions.quote: There have been reports of police asking victims of crime to provide vehicles for transportation, or money to buy fuel for police vehicles.

propositions.text: Recent RIRs indicate poor funding, low morale, lack of office space, personnel, facilities, and communication equipment for NPF
propositions.quote: A recent Response to Information Request (RIR)34 provides information regarding the poor funding for the NPF which has led to low morale amongst serving officers. The same RIR indicates that the police lack office space, personnel, and facilities for effective performance of its functions. According to another RIR,35 the IG of Police reportedly stated that one of the greatest challenges police are facing in Nigeria is a lack of adequate communication equipment.

propositions.text: IG of Police states funding and material inputs for crime prevention and investigation are inadequate
propositions.quote: The IG of police also indicated that material inputs in terms of funding, crime prevention/control, detection, investigation, traffic-control and accident prevention, communication and data-gathering research needs are inadequate.

propositions.text: RAD not persuaded Nigerian police are competent, equipped, or motivated to search for Appellants nationwide
propositions.quote: The RAD is not persuaded that the Nigerian police are competent and well enough equipped or motivated to search for the Appellants throughout the country.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no persuasive evidence Appellants are sought nationwide; NPF is under-resourced, ineffective, and unlikely to search for them.

propositions.text: Appellants failed to explain why they believe they would be discovered or harmed by NPF in Abuja or Port Harcourt
propositions.quote: Thus, the Appellants have failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why they believe they would be discovered and/or harmed by the NPF in Abuja, or Port Harcourt.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, Appellants could live in these cities without serious possibility of persecution
propositions.quote: Therefore, the RAD finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants could live in any of these three cities without serious possibility of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concludes Appellants failed to explain risk from NPF and could live in these cities without serious persecution risk.

propositions.text: RAD reviewed RPD's analysis and evidence and agrees with its findings
propositions.quote: The RAD has reviewed the RPD's analysis and the evidence which supports its findings and agrees with the findings made.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with the RPD's analysis and findings after review.

propositions.text: RAD concurs with RPD for stated reasons regarding second prong of IFA
propositions.quote: The RAD concurs with the RPD for the following reasons. The Appellant's psychological condition

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concurs with the RPD regarding the second prong of the IFA and the Appellant's psychological condition.

propositions.text: RAD conducted its own assessment of psychologist Dr. XXXX's report dated 2015
propositions.quote: The RAD conducted its own assessment of the psychological report36 of psychologist Dr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, dated XXXX XXXX, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD conducted its own assessment of the psychologist's 2015 report.

propositions.text: Appellants satisfy diagnostic criteria for stressor-related disorder with prolonged duration
propositions.quote: Dr. XXXX states that the Appellants satisfied diagnostic criteria for stressor-related disorder with prolonged duration.

propositions.text: RAD accepts psychologist's diagnosis but gives little weight to report for IFA viability
propositions.quote: The RAD accepts the diagnosis of the psychologist. However, the RAD gives little weight to the document as it relates to the viability of an IFA for the Appellants.

propositions.text: Appellant's mental state does not affect RAD's conclusions
propositions.quote: The Appellant's mental state does not affect the RAD's conclusions in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD accepts the diagnosis of stressor-related disorder but gives little weight to the report for IFA viability; mental state does not affect conclusions.

propositions.text: Psychological assessment was to accompany Appellant's request to stay in Canada
propositions.quote: Dr. XXXX states that the psychological assessment was completed to accompany the Appellant's request to stay in Canada.

propositions.text: Appellant had received no mental health treatment as of report date
propositions.quote: Dr. XXXX states that the Appellant requires mental-health treatment but that, as of the date of the report, the Appellant had received no such treatment.

propositions.text: Appellant provided no evidence of seeking mental health care after interview nine months before RPD hearings
propositions.quote: The Appellant provided no evidence that he sought mental-health care after his interview with Dr. XXXX which was conducted nine months before his hearings before the RPD.

propositions.text: No reason to believe report was written in ongoing therapeutic relationship context
propositions.quote: The RAD, therefore, has no reason to believe that the report was written in the context of an on-going therapeutic relationship between the author and the Appellant.

propositions.text: Appellant's failure to seek treatment suggests he does not take diagnosis seriously
propositions.quote: The Appellant's own actions in not seeking treatment for his mental health do not suggest that he takes seriously the diagnosis in the report.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the psychological report was not part of ongoing treatment; Appellant did not seek care, suggesting he does not take diagnosis seriously.

propositions.text: Dr. XXXX diagnosed Appellant with PTSD with dissociative symptoms per DSM-5
propositions.quote: Dr. XXXX provided the following information: Mr. XXXX (the Appellant's) satisfies diagnostic criteria for post trauma stress disorder (309.81[F43.10] with dissociative symptoms in the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., DSM-5).

propositions.text: Appellant requires mental health treatment including stress management and cognitive-behaviour therapy
propositions.quote: He requires mental-health treatment. Psychological treatment might include stress-management training, behavioral activation, and cognitive-behaviour therapy.

propositions.text: Appellant's condition will deteriorate with further threats of harm
propositions.quote: Mr. XXXX condition will deteriorate with exposure to further threats of harm.

paragraphs.summary: Dr. XXXX diagnosed Appellant with PTSD needing treatment; condition worsens with further threats.

propositions.text: Report has no probative value as only one 60-minute session occurred with no ongoing treatment
propositions.quote: The RAD finds this information has no probative value. There is nothing in the report to show that other than the 60 minutes that the male Appellant and the principal Appellant met with the doctor, no other sessions have taken place nor is there any evidence on any ongoing treatment.

propositions.text: No evidence Appellants are in any treatment programs
propositions.quote: It is clear that the entire assessment of both the male Appellant and the principal Appellant took place over a 60 minute session. There is no evidence before the RAD that the Appellants have been given any future treatment, what can be deciphered from the report is that neither Appellant are in any treatment programs.

propositions.text: RAD finds little probative value in Dr. XXXX's report
propositions.quote: As such the RAD finds little probative value in the report of Dr. XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the psychological report has little probative value due to only one session and no evidence of ongoing treatment.

propositions.text: UK Home Office report indicates mental health services in Nigeria are limited and underutilized due to ignorance and supernatural beliefs
propositions.quote: The UK Home Office report of June 14, 2013 (reissued February 3, 2014) indicates that mental health services are limited in Nigeria and often underutilized because of widespread ignorance and supernatural beliefs about the etiology of mental illness.

propositions.text: Psychiatric care in Nigeria is provided at few large mental hospitals in big cities
propositions.quote: Psychiatric care is provided at a few large mental hospitals in big cities.

propositions.text: Nigeria has eight federally funded psychiatric hospitals and six state-owned mental hospitals
propositions.quote: Nigeria's mental health facilities consist of eight federally funded psychiatric hospitals and six state-owned mental hospitals and managed by various state governments.

propositions.text: Primary care doctors and nurses authorized to prescribe psychotherapeutic medicines
propositions.quote: Primary Care Prescription regulations authorize primary health care doctors and nurses to prescribe and/or continue prescriptions for psychotherapeutic medicines.

propositions.text: Over thirty mental health drugs are available in Nigeria
propositions.quote: The report lists over thirty mental health drugs available in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes UK report that mental health services in Nigeria are limited, underutilized, with few hospitals and some drug availability.

propositions.text: On a balance of probabilities, the Appellants could access adequate mental-health care in Abuja or Port Harcourt.
propositions.quote: the RAD, therefore, finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants could access adequate mental-health care in Abuja, or Port Harcourt if they so choose.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellants could access adequate mental-health care in Abuja or Port Harcourt.

propositions.text: The RPD failed to apply the Chairperson Guidelines, breaching natural justice.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to apply the Chairperson Guidelines and this is a breach of natural justice.

propositions.text: The RAD disagrees and finds the RPD provided clear reasons applying the Chairperson Guidelines, no breach of natural justice.
propositions.quote: The RAD fully disagrees with this argument, and finds that the RPD provide fulsome and clear reasons on its application of the Chairpersons Guidelines.

propositions.text: The RPD clearly addressed both the Women's - Gender and the Children Refugee Guidelines, no breach of natural justice.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the RPD did not commit a breach of natural justice in this respect as it clearly addressed both the Women's - Gender and the Children Refugee Guidelines.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue the RPD breached natural justice by not applying Chairperson Guidelines; the RAD disagrees and finds no breach.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant and wife well educated with good employment potential to provide for themselves and minors in IFA locales.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant and his wife were well educated and had good employment potential and could, thus provide for themselves and the minor Appellants in the IFA locales.

propositions.text: The RPD referred to documents in the NDP about women and female children relocating within Nigeria needing physical protection.
propositions.quote: The RPD referred to a number of documents found within the NDP which refer specifically to women and female children relocating within Nigeria who require physical protection.

propositions.text: The RPD found resources available to vulnerable women and female children facing forced circumcision.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that there are resources available to vulnerable women and female children such as the wife and minor female Appellant facing forced circumcision.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellants well educated with resources available to vulnerable women and children facing forced circumcision.

propositions.text: The RPD did not consider documentary evidence about challenges of relocation for women in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD did not pay due consideration to particular documentary evidence which speaks to the challenges of relocation for women in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence indicates women relocating may face stigma and economic and social constraints.
propositions.quote: The Appellants referred to documentary evidence which indicates, for example, that women may be stigmatized in their new communities due to social and cultural constraints or that a woman who chooses to relocate could face a number of economic and social constraints depending upon her situation.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue the RPD ignored evidence about women's relocation challenges including stigma and constraints.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees with the RPD that the evidence refers to women relocating alone, not with husband as here.
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees with the RPD. The documentary evidence referred to by the Appellants in this regard refers specifically to the problems encountered by women relocating on their own or with their children, not a woman relocating with her husband.

propositions.text: The Appellants conflated women relocating alone with the Appellants' situation where wife relocates with husband and children.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellants have conflated the situation with women in Nigeria relocating on their own with the Appellants' situation where the wife would be relocating with her husband, the Appellant, and the minor Appellants.

propositions.text: The male Appellant would be present and protective of the wife and minor Appellants.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the male Appellant would be present and as such he would also be protective of the principal Appellant and the minor Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the relocation evidence applies to women alone, not the Appellants relocating as a family with male protection.

propositions.text: The Appellants could live in Abuja or Port Harcourt without fear or need to hide.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the RAD notes as per the RPD finding that the Appellants could live in any of the two cities without fear or the need to hide.

propositions.text: If Appellants do not inform others, their location would likely remain unknown; cities are large and distant from Lagos.
propositions.quote: If the Appellants do not wish to inform others of their presence in these cities, there is no reason to believe that their location would be found out. The RAD notes that the cities are large and located at a substantial distance from Lagos.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellants could live safely and discreetly in Abuja or Port Harcourt, large cities far from Lagos.

propositions.text: The record contains sufficient evidence to support that an IFA in Abuja or Port Harcourt is accessible to the Appellants.
propositions.quote: Based on the totality of the evidence, the RAD notes that the record contained sufficient evidence to support a finding that an IFA in Abuja or Port Harcourt is accessible to the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds sufficient evidence supports that an IFA in Abuja or Port Harcourt is accessible to the Appellants.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, no serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment exists for Appellants in these cities.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the RPD finding that on a balance of probabilities, that there is not a serious possibility of persecution of the Appellants in these cities, that their removal to Nigeria would not subject them personally to a risk to his life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture.

propositions.text: Appellants failed to provide sufficient evidence they would be discovered or harmed at these locations.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellants have failed to provide sufficient evidence as to why they believe they would be discovered and/or harmed at any of these locations, and therefore there is no reason to believe, on a balance of probabilities, that they would be harmed.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no serious risk of persecution or harm to Appellants in these cities; Appellants failed to prove otherwise.

propositions.text: Reasonableness of IFA is whether it is unduly harsh to expect claimants to move to less hostile part before seeking status abroad, per Thirunavukkarasu.
propositions.quote: The test for reasonableness is whether it would be unduly harsh to expect the claimants to move to another, less hostile part of the country before seeking status abroad, as per Thirunavukkarasu.

propositions.text: Thirunavukkarasu sets a high threshold; hardship of dislocation is not undue hardship making IFA unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Thirunavukkarasu sets a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable in all the circumstances. The hardship associated with dislocation and relocation is not the kind of undue hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable.

propositions.text: Dislike of weather, lack of friends or suitable work is insufficient to render IFA unreasonable.
propositions.quote: However, it is not enough for the Appellant to say that he or she does not like the weather there, or that he or she has no friends or relatives there, or that he or she may not be able to find suitable work there.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD explains the high legal threshold for IFA reasonableness, citing Thirunavukkarasu and what hardship does not suffice.

propositions.text: The RPD considered the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines regarding IFA.
propositions.quote: In considering the viability of the IFA, the RPD has given consideration to the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines, specifically as it relates to IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD considered the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines on IFA viability.

propositions.text: Gender Guidelines require considering women's ability to travel safely and stay at IFA without undue hardship.
propositions.quote: In determining the reasonableness of a woman's recourse to an internal flight alternative, decision-makers should consider the ability of women, because of their gender, to travel safely to the IFA and to stay there without facing undue hardship.

paragraphs.summary: The Gender Guidelines require assessing women's safe travel and stay at IFA without undue hardship.

propositions.text: The female Appellant receives strong support from her husband, mitigating gender-related hardship.
propositions.quote: The RAD takes note that the female Appellant has received and continues to receive strong support from her husband. He has demonstrated a commitment to the principal Appellant throughout the situation, and there is no reason to believe that he will not continue to provide her with ongoing support.

propositions.text: Any hardship from gender will be mitigated by husband's ongoing support.
propositions.quote: In light of that, the RAD finds that any hardship encountered by the principal Appellant arising from her gender will be mitigated by the fact that she will receive support from her husband.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the female Appellant's husband's support mitigates any gender-related hardship.

propositions.text: Appellants provided no persuasive evidence they would be unfamiliar with cultural norms in these cities.
propositions.quote: The Appellants provided no persuasive evidence that they would not be familiar with cultural issues and norms in these cities.

propositions.text: It would be reasonable for Appellants to adapt and obtain employment in these cities.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the RAD is satisfied that it would be reasonable for the Appellants to adapt to new surroundings in any of these cities and be able to obtain employment in her respective areas.

propositions.text: Many Nigerians establish support networks beyond family, including religious and social organizations.
propositions.quote: Many Nigerians try to establish other support networks that may complement or in some cases replace the extended family. Examples of such support networks are religious congregations, religious organizations, age grades/sets, political organizations, charities and guilds.

propositions.text: Appellants are practicing Christians; southern Nigeria is predominantly Christian; Abuja has both Muslims and Christians.
propositions.quote: The Appellants testified that they are practicing Christians. The documentary evidence states that the southern states of Nigeria (in which Ibadan is located) are predominantly Christian while both Muslims and Christians reside in large numbers in the Federal Capital Territory where Abuja is found.

propositions.text: Appellants have moral and spiritual support available in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: For this reason, the RAD is satisfied that the Appellants have sources of moral and spiritual assistance and support available to them in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellants can adapt culturally, obtain employment, and have moral and spiritual support in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Principal and minor Appellants have an IFA in Nigeria and do not face serious persecution or risk of cruel treatment or torture there.
propositions.quote: Given the finding above that the principal Appellant and the minor Appellants have an internal flight alternative in Nigeria, the RAD finds that the principal Appellant and the minor Appellants do not face a serious possibility of persecution there, and it also finds that their removal to Nigeria would not subject them personally to a risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the principal and minor Appellants have an IFA in Nigeria without serious risk of persecution or cruel treatment.

propositions.text: The Appellants have a viable IFA in Abuja or Port Harcourt.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Abuja, or Port Harcourt.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellants have a viable IFA in Abuja or Port Harcourt.

propositions.text: The child born in the U.S. is a U.S. citizen with rights and social safety nets there.
propositions.quote: With respect to the child born in the U.S., namely, XXXX XXXX XXXX, as he is a citizen of the United States, he enjoys the rights and privileges of that country. He would be able to benefit from the social safety networks of the U.S.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the U.S.-born child is a U.S. citizen with rights and social safety nets there.

propositions.text: No evidence was provided against the U.S. claiming persecution; the U.S. would protect the child if needed.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, counsel has not provided any evidence against the United States claiming persecution should he return, the RAD also notes that there is no claim against the U.S., who would protect him if he was in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no evidence of persecution claim against the U.S. and that the U.S. would protect the child.

propositions.text: The minor U.S.-born child is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection; appeal rejected.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I find that the minor child born in the U.S. is neither a Convention refugee, nor is he a person in need of protection. Therefore, I am rejecting his appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD rejects the appeal of the minor U.S.-born child as he is not a refugee or in need of protection.

propositions.text: The male Appellant is excluded under Article 1F (b).
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the male Appellant is excluded as per Article 1F (b).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the male Appellant excluded under Article 1F (b).

propositions.text: The principal Appellants and minor Appellants have a viable internal flight alternative in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the principal Appellants and XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX (the minor Appellants) have a viable internal flight alternative in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the principal and minor Appellants have a viable internal flight alternative in Nigeria.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the minor Appellant born in the U.S. is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection
propositions.quote: The RAD finds XXXX XXXX XXXX, minor Appellant born in the U.S. is neither a Convention refugee, nor is he a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the minor Appellant born in the U.S. is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal under section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA
propositions.quote: and dismisses the appeal in accordance with section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection and dismisses the appeal under section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal
propositions.quote: The RAD dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal.
